en: When building web applications, you may be
using SQLite, and an earlier lecture showed
you how you could use Bun's built-in SQLite
client for that. But if you're using a MySQL
or a PostgreSQL database, Bun also got you
covered because Bun includes a general SQL
client as well, in addition to that separate
SQLite client covered earlier.
As a side note, you can also use this SQL
client for SQLite, but you'll see that in
just a second.
Either way, it's built into Bun, no extra
packages needed, and it then allows you to
connect to a SQL database, a MySQL,
PostgreSQL, or SQLite database. It supports
connection pooling if the database server
supports it, and it makes creating and
executing SQL queries in a safe way,
protected against SQL injection attacks, a
breeze.
So to get started with Bun's built-in SQL
client, I'm back in that same SQLite project
I covered in earlier lectures.
In there, however, in DBTS, I'm no longer
using BUNN's SQLite client, which of course
you could use when working with SQLite, not
a bad idea, but I'm using its SQL client
because as mentioned, that also supports
SQLite as one of the supported database
engines.
Now, in order to use this SQL client, you
start by instantiating it by creating an
object based on it, so to say, where you can
specify your adapter. Now, as a side note,
you technically don't need to do that
because Bun will take a look at the other
hints it's getting, like for example, the
existence of a filename, which tells it that
it will be a SQLite database because for
MySQL and PostgreSQL, you would have a
server, you wouldn't have a filename there.
And for those databases, it would look at
the connection URL to determine whether it's
PostgreSQL or MySQL. But you can also
explicitly state the adapter here if you
want to. And at the point of time where
recording this, the supported databases are
SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL, and also
MariaDB. But in this course, I'll focus on
SQLite and then later also Postgres.
So SQLite, it is here. Then we have some
options which you may already know from the
SQLite lectures, whether the database file
should be created if it's not there, and
strict settings which do some extra checks
regarding parameters.
But the queries and SQL statements are then
executed in a different way than before
because instead of using that SQLite client,
we're now using the SQL client and we run
SQL queries through a special SQL tagged
template literal.
That is simply the thing we get back from
instantiating SQL, this SQL class here.
And that then may look a bit weird, but that
is an official JavaScript and therefore also
TypeScript feature.
You can think of it as a function that
receives a template literal as an input. And
the template literal content you pass in
there is simply the SQL command or query you
wanna execute. So here for SQLite, a pragma
statement for setting up WAL mode, so to
configure it,
then this create table statement for
creating a new table if it doesn't exist
yet,
and then also for creating an index.
And then later down below, also some extra
queries for getting notes, for example.
Now,
as mentioned, this SQL client also supports
SQL statements that receive parameters, SQL
queries that receive parameters, and it does
so in a way that automatically protects
against SQL injection attacks.
For example, here in getNode, we have the
same approach as before using the SQL tagged
template literal approach, but now in there
you see the ID is
inserted into that template literal. And
that may look unsafe at first because it
looks like we're just inserting whatever we
receive here as an input. So that could
potentially yield a SQL injection attack or
lead to a SQL injection vulnerability. But
that's not the case. This SQL tagged
template literal feature provided by Bun
will automatically sanitize the
input you're injecting into it and will
protect against those attacks. So this is
the safe way of inserting something dynamic
into the SQL statement.
And you cannot just do that here for your
parameters
when getting some data, but of course also,
for example, here for the values that you
may be inserting into a database with that
INSERT statement, which again is executed
with that SQL tagged template literal
feature. That is how you send all your
queries and statements to the database
except for transactions to which I'll get
back in just a second.
It's also worth noting that of course the
statements, the queries you run can return
data.
So you can get back a row that was fetched
here, for example, which is why SQL is a
generic function in the end and you define
the data you know you'll be getting back to
have type safety.
